content: Diarrhea remains one of the leading causes of preventable death in developing countries, particularly among children under the age of five. It is defined as an increase in the frequency of stools, such as more than three bowel movements per day, or the presence of loose stools compared to the normal consistency of stools. Acute diarrhea is classified as diarrhea lasting less than three weeks, while chronic diarrhea persists for more than three weeks. The hydration status of the child is a critical factor in managing diarrheal illnesses in pediatric patients. The risk of dehydration due to fluid and electrolyte losses is inversely proportional to the child’s age; younger children are at a higher risk of dehydration. The type of dehydration—whether isotonic, hypotonic, or hypertonic—is generally independent of the causative agent. Severe fluid loss from diarrhea and vomiting can become life-threatening if it reaches levels as high as three times the circulating blood volume (80–125–250 mL per kg of body weight per day). To maintain blood volume, the body compensates by extracting fluid from the intracellular space, which predisposes the child to dehydration. Complications and hospitalizations due to dehydration can often be prevented through the early and adequate oral administration of a rehydration solution (glucose-electrolyte solution) and the continuation of normal age-appropriate feeding. The causes of diarrhea can range from mild, self-limiting conditions to life-threatening illnesses. A focused initial rapid evaluation (FIRE) should be conducted to identify patients requiring immediate intervention. The diagnostic and treatment approaches for acute diarrhea in children are summarized in algorithms based on WHO guidelines. Do's: Ensure the child is well-hydrated. Proper hydration is essential for early recovery and the resolution of diarrheal symptoms. Encourage appropriate eating habits. A diet including bananas, rice, applesauce, and toast (commonly referred to as the BRAT diet) can be beneficial. Consider the use of probiotics, as they may help reduce the duration of the illness. Use antibiotics only when specifically indicated for pediatric diarrheal illnesses. Don'ts: Do not attempt to prepare homemade salt and fluid combinations unless instructed by a pediatrician and with the proper tools. Do not withhold food from the child if they are hungry. Do not use antibiotics unless prescribed by a pediatrician. Do not ignore symptoms; monitor and record the child’s temperature and hydration status regularly.
